resource.title: Resource characterization & modeling
resource.blurb: Geological surveys, geophysical data and exploration wells are used to map subsurface temperature, rock properties and permeability. This information guides well placement and helps estimate the resource’s potential flow rate and heat output.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS needs hot rock where wells can be connected through permeable or stimulated pathways. CLGS relies on heat transfer into sealed pipes. Superhot targets much higher temperatures and pressures.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Exploration methods are established, but predicting commercial well productivity remains difficult and requires confirmation through drilling and testing.

drilling.title: Drilling & well design
drilling.blurb: Drilling creates the injection and production wells that access the geothermal resource. Well depth, trajectory and completion design determine how effectively the wells connect to the reservoir. Drilling and completion are major project costs, accounting for 57% of modeled deep-EGS capital cost in NLR's 2025 market report.
kpis: Drilling cost per meter / days to drill

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS generally requires connected injection and production wells. CLGS requires sealed, often multilateral well loops. Superhot wells must withstand extreme temperatures and pressures.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven equipment; improving EGS-specific execution. Directional drilling and well construction are established, but geothermal hard-rock drilling remains costly. NLR estimates drilling and completion account for 57% of modeled deep-EGS overnight capital cost. FORGE reduced drilling time from 310 hours in 2020 to 110 hours in 2023.

reservoir.title: Reservoir creation & management
reservoir.blurb: Water is injected under pressure to create or expand fractures in hot rock, establishing pathways for circulation between injection and production wells. Operators manage flow and pressure to sustain heat extraction while limiting water loss and induced seismicity.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS relies on fluid flow through fractures in the rock. CLGS transfers heat through sealed pipe walls without circulating fluid through the formation. Superhot designs may use natural permeability or engineered pathways.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Field tests have demonstrated circulation through stimulated rock, but long-term performance and repeatability remain site-dependent. Utah FORGE demonstrated high flow rates and fluid recovery during 2024 testing; this is a research demonstration, not commercial operating history.

monitoring.title: Monitoring & instrumentation
monitoring.blurb: Downhole sensors, fiber-optic cables and seismic networks measure temperature, pressure, fluid flow and subsurface activity. These data help operators evaluate reservoir performance, monitor well conditions and adjust injection and production.
kpis: Seismic event count and maximum magnitude

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS monitoring emphasizes fracture flow, reservoir pressure, water loss and induced seismicity. CLGS focuses on loop temperature, pressure, flow and integrity. Superhot requires sensors that can survive extreme conditions.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Seismic monitoring and downhole sensing are established technologies and have been deployed at EGS test sites. Their ability to characterize complex reservoirs and predict long-term behavior remains limited by sensor coverage and subsurface uncertainty.

pumps.title: Production & injection pumps
pumps.blurb: Pumps circulate water between the surface and underground reservoir, maintaining the pressure and flow needed to extract heat. Their capacity and energy consumption affect both operating costs and net electricity generation.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS pumps move water into and out of a fractured reservoir. CLGS circulates fluid through a sealed loop. Superhot systems may require specialized fluid-handling equipment.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Industrial pumping equipment is mature. The project-specific challenge is matching pump performance to reservoir pressure, flow and fluid conditions.

plant.title: Heat exchangers & ORC generation
plant.blurb: Heat exchangers transfer energy from geothermal fluid to a secondary working fluid, which vaporizes and drives a turbine in an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC). ORC systems are commercially established and allow electricity generation from moderate-temperature resources.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS commonly uses binary ORC at moderate temperatures, though other cycles may suit hotter resources. CLGS generally uses ORC. Superhot systems may use direct steam where fluid conditions allow.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Binary geothermal plants are commercially deployed. The uncertainty is whether the reservoir supplies enough heat at sufficient temperature and flow to support expected output.

water.title: Cooling & water management
water.blurb: Cooling systems reject heat from the power cycle so the working fluid can be reused. Wet cooling uses water to improve heat rejection, while air cooling reduces water demand but can lower plant efficiency in hot conditions. Operators also track reservoir fluid losses and replacement-water needs.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: EGS manages both plant cooling demand and reservoir fluid losses. CLGS has a sealed underground loop, so reservoir water loss is not a comparable operating issue. Superhot systems face additional fluid-handling considerations.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Cooling equipment is established. The project-specific trade-off is between water use, capital cost and net generation; reservoir water loss is a separate EGS risk.

grid.title: Grid connection
grid.blurb: Substations, transformers and transmission lines connect the plant to the electricity grid. Interconnection requirements and available transmission capacity influence project development timelines and costs.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from CLGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: Grid equipment is similar across all three technologies. The main differences are expected plant output and location, not the interconnection technology.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Grid equipment is mature. Project-specific interconnection access, upgrade costs and transmission capacity remain material development risks.

resource.title: Resource exploration & modeling
resource.blurb: Exploration identifies deep rock formations with sufficiently high temperatures and pressures for superhot geothermal production. Geological and geophysical data help estimate resource depth, fluid conditions and potential well productivity, guiding where and how to drill.
kpis: Depth and temperature/pressure of the target

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Superhot targets much higher temperatures and pressures than conventional EGS or most CLGS projects. The challenge is confirming that the resource can be accessed and produce fluid at useful rates.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Exploration methods are established, but commercial superhot resources are not well characterized. Iceland’s IDDP-2 reached 427°C at 4,659 m and 340 bar, demonstrating access to extreme conditions—not sustained commercial production.

drilling.title: High-temperature drilling & well design
drilling.blurb: Specialized drilling tools, casing, cement and completion equipment are used to access and maintain wells at extreme temperatures and pressures. Material selection and well design are critical to reliability and can add significant cost compared with conventional geothermal wells.
kpis: Days and cost to target depth

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Superhot wells impose more severe temperature and materials requirements than typical EGS or CLGS wells. Specialized tools and well materials must maintain performance beyond conventional geothermal operating limits.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Early-stage for superhot conditions. Conventional drilling expertise provides a foundation, but long-term well integrity at superhot conditions is unresolved. ARPA-E’s SUPERHOT program targets robust wells capable of operating for 15 years or more.

reservoir.title: Reservoir access & fluid management
reservoir.blurb: Reservoir design and management establish pathways for fluid to reach hot rock and return to the surface. Depending on the geology, projects may use natural permeability or engineered stimulation. High-temperature fluids carry substantial thermal energy but may require specialized handling due to their chemistry and phase behavior.
kpis: Temperature and pressure decline over time

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Superhot designs may use natural or engineered permeability, depending on geology and project design. EGS typically creates or improves fracture connectivity. CLGS avoids formation-fluid circulation and transfers heat through sealed pipes.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Early-stage. Reaching superhot temperatures has been demonstrated, but sustained commercial fluid production and reservoir performance remain unproven. High temperature alone does not establish a productive resource.

monitoring.title: High-temperature monitoring
monitoring.blurb: High-temperature sensors measure downhole temperature, pressure, flow and well conditions. These measurements help operators assess resource performance, monitor well integrity and manage production under extreme operating conditions.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Superhot requires sensors and materials rated for much higher temperatures and pressures. EGS monitoring emphasizes fracture flow and seismicity; CLGS monitoring focuses on sealed-loop conditions and leak detection.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. High-temperature sensing technologies exist, but sustained reliability and coverage under superhot well conditions require further field validation.

pumps.title: Produced-fluid handling
pumps.blurb: Surface equipment separates steam from liquid, controls pressure and removes gases or dissolved minerals from produced geothermal fluid. Equipment materials and treatment processes are selected to handle high temperatures and potentially corrosive or mineral-rich fluids.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Superhot systems may require high-temperature separation, steam washing and corrosion-resistant equipment. EGS systems generally handle lower-temperature produced water; CLGS circulates a contained working fluid rather than producing reservoir fluid.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven as an integrated system. Separators and fluid-treatment equipment are established industrial technologies, but their materials and configuration must be matched to superhot geothermal fluid conditions.

plant.title: Turbines & power conversion
plant.blurb: Depending on fluid temperature, pressure and composition, superhot resources may support direct-steam power generation or a binary cycle. Direct-steam systems send produced steam through a turbine, while binary systems transfer heat to a separate working fluid. Turbine design must match the resource conditions.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: EGS and CLGS commonly use binary ORC systems. Superhot may use direct steam if resource conditions are suitable; the choice depends on fluid properties and plant design.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. CATF’s conceptual 500-MW plant study rated most assessed surface equipment at TRL 8–9, but its specialized steam turbine at TRL 5–6. The study estimated surface-plant capital cost at approximately $1,989/kW, excluding wellfield costs; this is a conceptual estimate, not a project quote.

water.title: Cooling & reinjection
water.blurb: Cooling systems lower the temperature of working fluids after power generation so they can be reused or reinjected. Wet cooling generally improves heat rejection but requires water, while dry cooling reduces water use and can increase auxiliary power demand. Reinjection also helps maintain reservoir pressure and fluid circulation.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: The cooling trade-off is similar across geothermal technologies. Superhot projects must also account for the chemistry and condition of produced fluid before reinjection. EGS additionally manages reservoir water losses; CLGS uses a sealed underground loop.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven equipment; project-specific fluid requirements. Cooling systems are established, but water demand and reinjection suitability depend on plant design and fluid chemistry.

grid.title: Grid connection
grid.blurb: Substations, transformers and transmission lines deliver electricity from the plant to the grid. Interconnection requirements, transmission availability and network upgrades affect project costs and the time needed to begin selling power.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and CLGS
differenceFrom.text: Grid equipment is similar across all three technologies. Higher expected output per superhot well does not remove the need for an available grid connection.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Electrical equipment is mature; interconnection access and upgrade requirements remain project-specific risks.

resource.title: Temperature mapping & thermal modeling
resource.blurb: Exploration measures the geothermal gradient, rock temperature and thermal properties used to estimate how much heat a closed-loop system can extract. Thermal models help guide well placement and loop geometry and predict output over the system's operating life.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS depends on temperature, rock thermal conductivity and heat transfer to the loop. EGS depends on connected fluid pathways through the reservoir. Superhot targets much higher temperatures and pressures.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Temperature mapping and thermal modeling are established, but predicting long-term heat output from a closed-loop design remains difficult and requires validation against operating systems.

drilling.title: Drilling, geometry & closed-loop piping
drilling.blurb: Drilling creates a sealed underground pipe network that circulates working fluid through hot rock. Horizontal and multilateral sections increase the pipe's contact area with the surrounding formation, improving heat exchange. Longer and more complex loops can increase drilling costs and construction time.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS uses connected, sealed pipe loops rather than separate injection and production wells circulating fluid through the formation. Some designs require extensive multilateral drilling.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Directional drilling is established, but deep multilateral closed-loop construction has limited commercial operating history. NREL modeling of Eavor Loop 2.0 found that an LCOE near $70/MWh required lateral drilling below about $400/m under specific assumptions; this is a modeled threshold, not a market price.

reservoir.title: Underground heat exchange
reservoir.blurb: Heat conducts from the surrounding rock through the pipe wall into the circulating fluid. The amount of heat collected depends on rock temperature and conductivity, pipe surface area, loop geometry and fluid flow. Increasing loop length can improve heat extraction but also increases drilling cost.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS transfers heat through sealed pipes. EGS brings fluid into direct contact with fractured rock; superhot systems produce fluid from extremely hot formations.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven; key performance uncertainty. The central question is whether the loop can extract enough heat per meter drilled to justify its capital cost. Long-term thermal drawdown also affects output.

monitoring.title: Sensors & leak monitoring
monitoring.blurb: Temperature, pressure and flow sensors track circulation and heat transfer throughout the closed loop. Pressure and flow measurements can also help identify leaks or changes in system performance, supporting maintenance and long-term operation.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS monitoring focuses on the sealed loop’s temperature, pressure, flow and integrity. EGS adds reservoir flow distribution, water loss and induced seismicity. Superhot requires instrumentation that can withstand extreme temperatures.

proven.heading: Partially Proven Technology
proven.text: Partially proven. Sensors and monitoring methods are established, but long-term performance in deep, complex closed-loop systems has less operating history. Avoiding reservoir stimulation reduces one source of induced-seismicity risk, but does not eliminate subsurface risk.

pumps.title: Circulation pumps
pumps.blurb: Pumps circulate working fluid through the underground loop and surface power plant. Pump capacity and pipe dimensions determine the flow rate and pressure required; friction losses in long loops affect pumping energy and net electricity output.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS circulates fluid within a sealed loop. EGS pumps inject and produce water through a fractured reservoir. Superhot systems may require specialized equipment to handle produced fluids.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven equipment. Industrial pumps are mature, but loop length, pipe diameter and flow rate determine pumping requirements and net output.

plant.title: Heat exchangers & ORC generation
plant.blurb: Heat exchangers transfer energy from the hot closed-loop fluid to a secondary working fluid, which drives a turbine in an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC). The ORC converts the collected geothermal heat into electricity, with performance largely determined by the temperature and flow rate delivered from underground.
kpis: Drilling share of project cost / LCOE

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS generally uses a binary cycle because its underground fluid remains inside a sealed loop. EGS commonly uses binary ORC at moderate temperatures. Superhot resources may support direct steam where fluid conditions allow.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven surface technology; resource-side performance less proven. ORC equipment is commercially established, but project economics depend on whether the underground loop supplies sufficient temperature and heat flow.

water.title: Cooling & fluid management
water.blurb: Cooling systems condense the ORC working fluid after it passes through the turbine so it can be circulated again. Air-cooled condensers reduce water use, while wet cooling can improve heat rejection. Cooling design affects plant efficiency, water demand and operating costs.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: CLGS has a sealed underground loop, so reservoir water loss is not a major operating issue. EGS must manage water losses from the reservoir. Superhot systems may also need to cool and reinject produced fluids.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Cooling equipment is mature; the main trade-off is water use versus performance and parasitic power.

grid.title: Grid connection
grid.blurb: Substations, transformers and transmission lines connect the power plant to the electricity grid. Interconnection costs and transmission access are important project considerations, particularly because the economics of closed-loop systems depend on maximizing net electricity output relative to drilling costs.

differenceFrom.heading: Difference from EGS and Superhot
differenceFrom.text: Grid equipment is the same as for EGS and superhot. For CLGS, the key project question is whether net output justifies drilling and interconnection costs.

proven.heading: Proven Technology
proven.text: Proven technology. Electrical equipment is mature; grid access, upgrade costs and interconnection timelines remain project-specific risks.
